title: Playing shop at home: prices, numbers and please in two languages
description: Line up a few tins and boxes from the cupboard, use paper squares as money, and play shop. Your child asks for things and counts out prices in the language you are building.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: Playing shop at home: prices, numbers and please in two languages
body:
Children love playing shop, and a pretend shop needs nothing you do not already own. It is also one of the few games where a child has to ask for something politely and count at the same time.

Set up the shop on a table or a low shelf with five or six things from the cupboard: a tin, a box of pasta, an apple, a piece of bread, a carton of milk. Give each one a price by saying it, not writing it — one, two or three. Keep every price under five.

For money, tear paper into small squares. Dried pasta works too once your child is past the age of putting things in their mouth.

Your child is the shopkeeper first; you are the customer. The script is short, and it runs in the language you are building. If that is Spanish: "Buenos días." "Buenos días." "Una manzana, por favor." "Aquí tiene." "¿Cuánto cuesta?" "Cuesta dos." "Gracias." "De nada."

If you are building English, the same exchange: "Good morning." "Good morning." "An apple, please." "Here you are." "How much is it?" "It's two." "Thank you." "You're welcome."

Then swap roles. As the customer, your child has to ask for what they want and count out the price, and that is where most of the talking happens.

Once the script is easy, add a small complication: the shopkeeper names a price that is too high, or runs out of apples. "No hay manzanas" / "there are no apples". Children enjoy a small problem, and solving it means reaching for new words.

The game lasts as long as your child wants it to. Five minutes is fine. If a soft toy or a grandparent joins as a second customer, even better: more customers, more please and thank you.

Close the shop with one last round: name each item as it goes back into the cupboard. "El pan, la leche, la manzana" — or "the bread, the milk, the apple".
